GS Area: GS2 Polity – Right to Privacy; GS3 – Data Governance
CA Topic / Headline: Kerala HC directs the Centre to make the Data Protection Board under the DPDP Act, 2023 functional within eight weeks, on a PIL over airport passenger data; Digi Yatra cannot insist on Aadhaar, and the court expects Voter ID to be accepted as proof.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• The PIL sought processing of passengers' personal data at airports in compliance with the DPDP Act, 2023 and the DPDP Rules, 2025.
• Digi Yatra Foundation told the court it accepts the driver's licence along with Aadhaar as proof of identity for facial-recognition boarding.
• The DPDP Act labels entities deciding why and how personal data is processed as Data Fiduciaries; the Data Protection Board adjudicates breaches and imposes penalties.
• Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v Union of India (2017) held privacy a fundamental right under Article 21; the Srikrishna Committee (2018) drafted the first data protection bill.
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Issue] Without a functioning Board, the Act's rights (consent, correction, erasure, grievance) cannot be enforced, leaving facial-recognition and financial-transaction trails unregulated.
• [Intro data] Every digital payment leaves a trace that can reveal tastes, habits and priorities; the Moneywise column calls the DPDP Act a form of 'digital armour'.
• [Counterpoint] Broad State exemptions (Section 17) and Centre-appointed Board members raise independence concerns; voluntary Digi Yatra still nudges biometric capture.
• [Way forward] Notify an independent Board quickly, purpose-limit airport biometrics, offer non-biometric alternatives and periodic audits of Data Fiduciaries.

GS Area: GS3 S&T – Emerging Tech; GS4 – Ethics of Surveillance
CA Topic / Headline: Norway proposes a temporary ban on smart glasses in sensitive public spaces (schools, playgrounds, healthcare facilities, locker rooms, beaches, parks, museums) over covert recording and real-time facial recognition, without banning sales or private use; Oslo has already banned them in municipal schools.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• Initiative led by Norway's Minister of Digitalisation and Public Governance Torgeir Micaelsen; an expert committee will frame lasting legal rules.
• Retailer Hans Anders suspended sales of Meta's Ray-Ban smart glasses in Dutch and Belgian stores pending guidance from the European Data Protection Board (EDPB).
• UK Cinema Association guidelines restrict camera glasses in theatres; courts in England and Wales require visitors to surrender them at security.
• Ray-Ban Meta glasses carry a white LED that blinks during photos and stays lit during video; firmware disables the camera if the LED is covered.
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Ethics] Smartphones signal recording when held up; eye-level ambient recording removes bystanders' cue to consent, creating diffuse surveillance.
• [Issue] Combined with real-time facial recognition, wearables could let strangers identify people instantly, access personal data or enable doxxing.
• [Counterpoint] Advocates of innovation say usage curbs cut device utility and sales; hardware safeguards and privacy-by-design may suffice.
• [Way forward] Geofenced recording-off zones, AI face-blurring before storage, blocked facial-recognition APIs and audio-only variants, as manufacturers are already exploring.

GS Area: GS3 Internal Security – Anti-terror Laws; GS2 – Rule of Law
CA Topic / Headline: On G.N. Saibaba's second death anniversary, lawyer Gautam Bhatia argues the UAPA's vague offences, near-impossible bail and inconsistent judicial interpretation imprison dissent: Bhima Koregaon trial yet to begin eight years on; Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam held over six years without trial.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• Saibaba was arrested under the UAPA in 2014, convicted to life imprisonment in 2017, acquitted by the Bombay High Court in 2024 after a decade in prison, and died soon after release.
• Bhima Koregaon (2018): UAPA charges against 16 scholars and activists; Father Stan Swamy died in custody; charges not yet framed.
• In 2011 an SC Bench read 'membership' of an unlawful organisation as 'active membership' involving incitement to violence; in 2023 the SC overturned this in review jurisdiction.
• In early 2026 the SC granted bail to five of seven Delhi riots appellants but denied it to Sharjeel Imam and Umar Khalid as 'intellectual architects'.
• Section 43D(5) of the UAPA bars bail if, on the chargesheet, accusations appear prima facie true (NIA v Zahoor Ahmad Shah Watali, 2019).
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Issue] Vague definitions plus the prima facie bail bar make the process the punishment; the Delhi HC's narrowing of 'terrorism' was declared non-precedent by the SC.
• [Judgment] Union of India v K.A. Najeeb (2021): prolonged incarceration and trial delay can justify bail under Article 21 despite statutory bars; courts apply it inconsistently.
• [Counterpoint] The State argues terror cases need stringent bail norms to protect witnesses and national security; low conviction rates partly reflect complex trials.
• [Way forward] Precise statutory definitions, time-bound trials, periodic review of detention, compensation for wrongful incarceration and data on UAPA outcomes.

CA Topic / Headline: As the RTI Act completes 21 years, a Hindu data analysis finds weak suo motu disclosure under Section 4: only 1,446 of 2,303 public authorities filed third-party transparency audits for 2024-25 (62.7%), and only 33 of 94 department websites carried audit reports.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• Section 4(1)(b) of the RTI Act lists 16 types of information, from officials' contact details to budgetary expenditure, to be disclosed suo motu.
• DoPT guidelines add disclosure under eight broad categories, including procurement, PPPs and all RTI applications received; transparency audits by third parties are shared with the CIC.
• Of the PAs that submitted audits, over 50% scored Grade C or below (80% or less); about 37% did not submit; submissions rose from 754 in 2020-21.
• Of 94 departments, 56 (62%) complied on most Section 4 categories; 26 department websites lacked the information; the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment had none.
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Issue] Poor proactive disclosure pushes citizens to file requests, swelling pendency at the CIC and State Information Commissions.
• [Intro data] The Act asks PAs to give 'as much information suo motu' so that the public need minimum resort to the Act.
• [Counterpoint] Departments cite thousands of websites and capacity gaps; voluntary disclosures must also respect Section 8 exemptions and the DPDP Act amendment to Section 8(1)(j).
• [Way forward] Mandatory machine-readable Section 4 dashboards, audit-linked rankings, CIC monitoring powers and penalties for chronic non-compliance.

GS Area: GS1 Post-Independence – Integration of Princely States; GS3 – NE Insurgency
CA Topic / Headline: Seven banned Meitei armed groups (six in the CorCom umbrella plus the Socialist Revolutionary Party) call a 12-hour shutdown on October 15 as 'National Black Day' against Manipur's 1949 merger with India, alleging King Bodhchandra signed under duress.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• The Manipur Merger Agreement was signed in Shillong on September 21, 1949 by Maharaja Bodhchandra Singh; it took effect on October 15, 1949.
• CorCom constituents: Kangleipak Communist Party, Kanglei Yawol Kanna Lup, PREPAK, PREPAK-Pro, Revolutionary People's Front and United National Liberation Front.
• The groups cite Article 2(4) of the UN Charter, the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, the Manipur State Constitution Act, 1947 and the Indian Independence Act, 1947.
• Manipur became a Part C State, then a Union Territory (1956) and a full State on January 21, 1972 under the North-Eastern Areas (Reorganisation) Act, 1971.
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Issue] Contested accession narratives (Manipur, as in Nagaland) sustain insurgent ideology and shutdown politics decades after integration.
• [Intro data] Manipur had held elections under its own Manipur State Constitution Act, 1947 before the merger, which fuels the 'illegal merger' claim.
• [Counterpoint] The Union holds the merger a valid instrument of a sovereign ruler; the Constitution and later statehood gave Manipur democratic self-government.

GS Area: GS3 Environment – Climate Change and Biodiversity
CA Topic / Headline: A Science Advances study on Hungarian agile frogs finds heat-driven sex reversal (genetic females developing as fertile males) lowers paternity and offspring fitness; sex-reversed males are about 20% of wild populations but sire only 4% of clutches.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• Around 40% of amphibian species face extinction risk, making them the most threatened vertebrates.
• In agile frogs, as in mammals, XX is female and XY male; excessive heat at the tadpole stage turns some XX tadpoles into fertile males.
• 61% of offspring of sex-reversed males underwent sex reversal, against 17% of offspring of sex-concordant males; under heat, their tadpoles carried higher ranavirus loads.
• Models show some populations could vanish in 60 to 70 years; with ranavirus, extinction came about 9.5 years sooner.
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Issue] Warming skews sex ratios, cuts effective breeding numbers and genetic diversity, raising extinction risk in small populations.
• [Intro data] Ranavirus has wiped out more than 90% of tadpoles in single events.
• [Counterpoint] Theory suggests XX males siring all-XX offspring can buffer warming up to a point, but only if they reproduce successfully.
• [Way forward] Monitor sex ratios genetically, protect cool breeding microhabitats, track disease, and include amphibians in climate adaptation plans.

Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Issue] Article 324 envisages a multi-member Commission; if the CEC acts without the other Commissioners' concurrence, decisions lose legitimacy, so recorded reasons and minutes become the test of collective functioning.

• [Counterpoint] The Commission says reports show only one part of the picture, that differences of opinion are normal in deliberative processes and that its decisions were unanimous.
• [Way forward] Publish minutes with dissent notes, notify rule changes before using revised forms, and commission the independent audit of SIR deletions that the petition seeks.

• [Counterpoint] Union Agriculture Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan said even meeting the CJI follows a procedure, and called the march drama.

GS Area: GS2 Polity – Fundamental Rights (Art 19); Delhi Governance
CA Topic / Headline: Delhi Police denotify Jantar Mantar as a designated protest site and name Ramlila Maidan, Burari Ground and CBD Ground; Express explainer lays out Article 19, Article 239AA(3)(a) and case law on regulating protest sites.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• Under Article 239AA(3)(a) the Delhi Assembly cannot legislate on public order, police and land, so Delhi Police work under the MHA, which set up the committee behind the new venues.
• In Ram Manohar Lohia (1966) the Court described law and order, public order and security of the State as three concentric circles, with public order narrower than law and order.
• Himat Lal Shah (1972) allowed prior permission for street meetings but not a total ban; Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan (2018) allowed earmarked areas and kept a limited part of Jantar Mantar Road open.
• Jantar Mantar became the protest site after the Boat Club Lawns were sealed in 1993; Burari is 16 km and CBD Ground over 26 km from it.
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Issue] Moving protests to distant grounds dilutes their purpose, the very concern accepted in MKSS (2018), where petitioners argued Ramlila Maidan was too far from the "concentration of power".
• [Judgment] Senior Advocate Gopal Sankaranarayanan says law and order alone cannot restrict speech; a law must give police the power and they must identify it.
• [Counterpoint] Trade body CTI says Ramlila protests would hit markets, claiming Rs 2,000 crore of business was lost on October 10, while the New Delhi Traders Association welcomed the shift.
• [Way forward] Publish SOPs, keep a small regulated site near Parliament, give written reasons for denials, and legislate a statutory protest framework.

• The CJI noted household tap connections in rural areas; water contaminated with arsenic or fluoride is a threat to life and health, not a service.

• [Judgment] Article 21 now imposes positive duties: the question is no longer only what the State must refrain from doing, but what it must ensure so people live with dignity.

• [Counterpoint] Human rights commissions only recommend and often lack enforcement teeth, so their credibility depends on being heard by those least able to make themselves heard.
• [Way forward] Courts intervene on violations, commissions investigate systemic failures, and governments publish water-quality data; protect aquifers and rivers for posterity.

CA Topic / Headline: Karnataka High Court strikes down Sections 3 and 4 of the SC/ST reservation Act, 2022 that took total quota to 56 per cent (SC 15 to 17, ST 3 to 7), holding the 50 per cent Indra Sawhney ceiling was breached.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• Section 3 was struck for violating Articles 14 and 15 and Section 4 for violating Articles 14 and 16; the Act took effect retrospectively from November 1, 2022.
• Petitioners argued the Act contravenes Indra Sawhney, a nine-judge bench that fixed the 50 per cent ceiling under Articles 15(4) and 16(4), with a narrow exception for extraordinary situations.
• They also said the National Commissions for SCs and STs were not consulted as Articles 338(9) and 338A(9) require; the Court said consultation must precede the decision.
• The State relied on the Nagamohan Das Commission, the Adi Committee and a 2017 backwardness report that said over 90% of the population is SC, ST or OBC.
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Judgment] The bench held a government's subjective view that a class is not adequately represented does not allow exceeding 50 per cent, which can be breached only in extraordinary situations.
• [Issue] Quotas above 50% need empirical, commission-backed findings and prior consultation; later consultation, nearly three years after the Act, does not cure the defect.
• [Counterpoint] Reserved-class members can still compete for the remaining unreserved pool, so the ceiling does not exclude them from open positions.
• [Way forward] Seek Supreme Court clarity on 'extraordinary situations', collect contemporaneous data on representation, and consult the national commissions before legislating.

CA Topic / Headline: Retail inflation rises to 5.54% in September from 4.83%, the highest in the new series; food inflation is 7.74% and core 4.3%. The RBI had raised the repo rate by 25 bps to 5.5% and projects inflation near 6% for October-December.

• 5.54% is the highest in the new series that starts January 2026; against the old 2012-base series it is the highest in almost two years, after 6.21% in October 2024.
• The RBI is mandated to keep inflation at 4% within a 2-6% band; September was the fourth straight month above 4%, and the repo was raised 25 bps to 5.5%.

• [Counterpoint] Supply-driven food and fuel inflation responds slowly to rate hikes, while tightening risks growth; kharif arrivals will decide the food path.
• [Way forward] Combine calibrated rate action with supply measures, buffer stock release, import duty cuts and clear forward guidance.

GS Area: GS3 Economy – Fiscal and Monetary Policy
CA Topic / Headline: Robert E Hall and Michael Woodford share the 2026 Economics Nobel for the microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation; the Express editorial and explainer link it to the RBI's rate hike and India's tax cuts.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• The prize of 12 million Swedish kronor (about Rs 12 crore) is shared; the citation reads 'for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation'.
• Hall worked on the demand side and used household microdata in 1982 to show hand-to-mouth households do not raise consumption on future income expectations.
• Woodford worked on the supply side: firms look ahead when fixing prices, so expectations about future interest rates matter and central banks must communicate intentions clearly.
• After the 1929 crash US GDP fell by 30% and unemployment reached 25%; the 1970s oil shocks produced stagflation, discrediting simple Keynesian intervention.
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Intro data] The Express ties the work to India's tax cuts in direct and indirect taxes during Covid and the RBI's recent rate hike to contain oil-driven inflation.
• [Issue] Stabilisation policy must handle trade-offs: cutting rates boosts demand but may raise inflation, while tightening to cut inflation can deepen unemployment.
• [Counterpoint] Letting markets self-correct could let inflation soar and hurt the poor most, forcing them to cut spending to essentials, as the explainer argues.
• [Way forward] Combine credible, transparent central bank communication with targeted fiscal support rather than blunt stimulus.

• Unapproved HT and next-generation Bt genes were present in over half of samples from 16 districts of Maharashtra, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh and Rajasthan.
• Manual weeding costs Rs 12,000-15,000 per acre against Rs 750-850 for two or three rounds of glyphosate; Vip3A has a different mode of action and works against pink bollworm.

• [Counterpoint] Environmental and health critics warn that unregulated herbicide-tolerant crops spread resistant weeds and contaminate non-GM fields, so blocking trials was precaution, not only ideology.

CA Topic / Headline: Ex-TRAI chairman's op-ed: PM-WANI public Wi-Fi, cabinet-approved in December 2020, has about 4 lakh hotspots because of costly backhaul; he proposes BharatNet, which has absorbed over Rs 48,000 crore and reached over 2 lakh panchayats, act as a common carrier.

• India has around 4 lakh public hotspots against over 13 million in France; BharatNet began in 2011 to connect 2.5 lakh gram panchayats.

• [Issue] A small PDO pays more for fibre than a household does, destroying the shopkeeper's economics; BharatNet is a pipe without taps.
• [Counterpoint] Mobile data is cheap, but bundled monthly plans exclude the poorest and students sharing a family data plan; public Wi-Fi also runs on unlicensed spectrum, sparing congested mobile networks.

• The NITI Aayog member puts GERD at Rs 2,44,767.81 crore in 2023-24, about 0.84% of GDP, with the private share up from 32.2% to 45.2%.

• [Issue] The two op-eds cite different GERD shares (0.64% and 0.84%), but both show spending far below peers; business funds about 40% in India against around three-quarters in the US and China.
• [Counterpoint] Pressure to commercialise research underinvests in discovery; a diagnostic platform may need years of disease biology before a product, so technology cannot be produced on demand.

• [Issue] The Adi community fears loss of ancestral land and livelihoods, and heavy security with arrests has stoked fears, so consent and rehabilitation determine legitimacy.

• [Intro data] Strategic logic: downstream storage would moderate sudden releases; NITI Aayog in 2017 proposed replacing Stage-I and Stage-II projects with one large storage project.
• [Way forward] Hold transparent public consultation with free, prior and informed consent, an independent cumulative impact assessment, and a binding data-sharing agreement with China.

CA Topic / Headline: Chhattisgarh's Devgaon village hired a 'guard' paid 2 kg of rice per household a month to drive away langurs; a viral video led to unverified claims that 22 langurs were shot, prompting a Forest Department probe into the hunter, whose gun was seized.

• Section 163 of the BNSS retains the spirit of Section 144 CrPC, 1973 and empowers a District Magistrate, SDM or specially empowered Executive Magistrate.

• [Issue] Preventive detention pre-empts future harm rather than punishing past offence; Rowlatt Act, 1919 and Defence of India Act, 1939 targeted freedom fighters, MISA targeted opponents in the Emergency (1975-77).

• [Counterpoint] Prolonged detention without trial, inadequate judicial oversight and potential misuse keep raising the balance between national security and fundamental rights.
• [Way forward] Enforce Article 22 safeguards strictly: prompt grounds, effective representation and time-bound Advisory Board review.

CA Topic / Headline: Delhi's Power Department notification of September 30 makes Aadhaar mandatory for domestic consumers to avail the electricity subsidy; those without Aadhaar can use the Enrolment ID; a CAG report found the scheme's cost rose from ₹2,405.59 crore in 2019-20 to ₹3,161 crore in 2022-23.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• The subsidy runs through five discoms: BSES Rajdhani, BSES Yamuna, Tata Power Delhi Distribution, NDMC and Military Engineer Services; spending comes from the Consolidated Fund of Delhi.
• The notification sets no deadline for existing beneficiaries and no separate procedure for consumers already receiving the benefit.
• Section 7 of the Aadhaar Act, 2016 allows Aadhaar for subsidies funded from the Consolidated Fund of India; the 2018 Puttaswamy judgment upheld it but struck down Section 57.
• The CAG report tabled in August says the scheme accounted for up to 70.39% of Delhi's total subsidy expense.
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Issue] Aadhaar linkage aims to simplify delivery, cut multiple identity documents and promote transparency; the risk is exclusion of households without Aadhaar or facing authentication failures.

• [Counterpoint] Targeting savings can be offset by exclusion errors, and the notification offers no route beyond the Enrolment ID.
• [Way forward] Allow alternate IDs, a grace period and grievance redress for existing beneficiaries to prevent exclusion.

CA Topic / Headline: Op-ed by physician Chandrakant Lahariya: overtreatment and overmedication stem from cascading tests, specialist fragmentation, marketised care, fee-for-service, insurance moral hazard, patient expectations and defensive medicine; he urges primary care, prescription review dates and Indian Choosing Wisely lists.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• A Frontiers in Pharmacology (2021) meta-analysis of Indian studies found polypharmacy in about 49% of older adults; a Scientific Reports (2025) study found potentially inappropriate medicines in 28.8% of cases.
• Choosing Wisely: between 2012 and 2023 nearly 80 specialty societies worldwide published close to 700 recommendations identifying low-value tests and treatments.
• A National Medical Journal of India review (2016) found routine health-check packages often include unwarranted tests leading to false positives and overdiagnosis.
• Health insurance can create ex-ante and ex-post moral hazard, discouraging preventive care and favouring costlier interventions.
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Issue] Overtreatment coexists with undertreatment: some get unnecessary interventions while many lack essential primary care, affordable medicines and timely treatment.
• [Counterpoint] Several medicines do not always mean overtreatment; the aim is structured medication review and deprescribing, not denying care.
• [Way forward] Rebuild primary care with the family physician as first contact; add review and stop dates to prescriptions; ICMR and societies to draw India-specific low-value care lists; pay for outcomes, not volume.
• [Ethics] Restraint is an ethical duty: informed consent includes the option of watchful waiting, and reassurance should not be mistaken for inaction.

GS Area: GS2 Polity – Judiciary; Prisons; Legal Aid
CA Topic / Headline: Data Point: India's incarceration rate is about 41 per 1,00,000, yet over three-quarters of prisoners in 2022 were undertrials; in a Maharashtra legal-aid programme 84% of bail applications succeeded against 26% in district courts, but participants spent 171 days in jail before intake.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• India ranks fourth in the world in the share of undertrials in its prison population; the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 created NALSA to provide free legal services to weaker sections.
• The programme, run since 2018 across eight Maharashtra prisons by Prayas (TISS) and the Fair Trial Fellowship (NLU Delhi), assisted over 22,000 undertrials between 2018 and 2023.
• Before intake 1% to 6% of participants had bail; after intake 61% to 92%; those released spent a further 115 days in custody.
• In 2018, about 37% of Maharashtra's 26,898 undertrials had been held for more than a year.
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):

• [Judgment] Rajesh Mihir Shah (2025): grounds must be communicated in writing, in a language the arrestee understands, orally if urgent and in writing at least two hours before remand; non-compliance makes arrest and remand illegal.

• [Judgment] In Jaskaran Jeet Singh Deol (September 2026), the investigating agency needs the magistrate's permission to re-arrest, and the court recommended departmental action and a change of investigating officer.
• [Way forward] Standardise a written grounds-of-arrest memo in the accused's language, record the time of service and make compliance auditable at the remand stage.

Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• AIFs are privately pooled investment vehicles raising capital from institutional and high-net-worth investors; SEBI regulates them under a framework separate from retail investment products.
• Accredited investors may invest in unlisted securities and other non-traditional assets that are complex, potentially illiquid and higher risk.
• SEBI's August 2026 consultation paper (Proposal 6) would admit individuals with at least ₹5 crore and companies with at least ₹20 crore invested in securities.

Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Issue] Widening the pool of accredited investors deepens private capital but pushes complex, illiquid products toward wealthier households that carry higher risk.
• [Counterpoint] Lower eligibility thresholds can invite mis-selling, so protection must rely on disclosure, not only on wealth.
• [Way forward] Pair easier eligibility with verification, risk disclosure and periodic review of AIF valuation and liquidity.

CA Topic / Headline: Op-ed: Safe in India Foundation finds 'unskilled' auto workers earning under ₹8,000 lost 2.27 fingers per accident in 2024 against 1.54 for skilled workers; the Code on Wages requires skill to be weighed in minimum wages.

CA Topic / Headline: Hall and Woodford's Nobel in Economics 'for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation' prompts an explainer contrasting the New Keynesian orthodoxy of sticky prices with the Keynes-Kalecki view that demand, particularly private investment, shapes both cycle and trend.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford received the 2026 Nobel in Economics for the microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation.
• In the New Keynesian Model, money is non-neutral only in the short run because prices are sticky; monetary policy primarily stabilises inflation, hence inflation targeting.
• Real business cycle theory was developed by Finn Kydland and Edward Prescott, who won the 2004 Nobel Prize in Economics.
• Kalecki held that the long-run trend is a slowly changing component of short-period situations; the golden age of capitalism ran from 1945 to 1973.
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Issue] The Keynes-Kalecki view says unemployment arises from inadequate private investment, not rigid prices, so public investment fills the gap when private investment is weak.
• [Counterpoint] Orthodox models hold that demand matters for the cycle but not the trend, which limits policy to the short run.
• [Issue] Authors argue the shift toward inflation targeting coincided with falling wage shares and a heavier burden on workers.
• [Way forward] Use fiscal and monetary tools jointly, and judge frameworks by their distributional impact on wages and employment.

CA Topic / Headline: Forest Rights Act title holders await a notification on the extra 50 days of work they had under MGNREGA, as the VB-G RAM G Act guarantees 125 days per household with no FRA tier; the Rural Development Ministry says no order exists.

• The Viksit Bharat-Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act (VB-G RAM G), rolled out on July 1, guarantees 125 days of wage employment per rural household in a financial year.
• Section 5(4) lets the Centre or a State provide work beyond the guaranteed days within its economic capacity; Section 7 allows relaxations during natural calamities.
• Under MGNREGA the additional 50 days for FRA title holders began in January 2014; 50 days for drought-prone areas had been introduced in 2012.
• In 2025-26 only 15% of the 14 lakh households eligible for 150 days under MGNREGA availed the benefit; Odisha had 3,72,089 registered households, the highest.
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Issue] Without a notification, FRA households may receive only 125 days, on a par with others, rather than 175 days including the earlier additional 50 days.
• [Counterpoint] The Ministry says a notification approving the additional 50 days is coming and six months remain in the financial year to use them.
• [Issue] Implementation was patchy even under MGNREGA: Andhra Pradesh was the only State that performed well, while Maharashtra's 96,559 registered households produced 8,063 beneficiaries.
• [Way forward] Notify the FRA entitlement, pre-register eligible households and track take-up in the MIS to ensure the extra days reach Adivasi households.

CA Topic / Headline: Bauxite mining proposal covering 147 hectares in Odisha's Balda hills, within the Nageswari reserve forest, threatens the Jeypore ground gecko, rediscovered in 2010 after 130 years; four individuals were documented in the past year and Bondo and Porja Adivasis protest.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• The Jeypore ground gecko, about 3.6 inches long, was first documented by Richard Henry Beddome in 1878 and rediscovered in 2010 in Odisha's Koraput district by Ishan Agarwal and Aniruddha Datta-Roy.
• The species lives only in high-elevation forests (900-1,400 metres) of the Eastern Ghats in Odisha and Andhra Pradesh.
• Potangi in Odisha, where the gecko was first sighted in the 1870s, has been lost to bauxite mining by the National Aluminium Company Limited (NALCO).
• The proposed open-cast bauxite mine of Kalinga Alumina Ltd., an Adani subsidiary, covers 147 hectares in the Nageswari reserve forest of the Balda hills.
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Issue] Habitat loss from mining is the main threat; the gecko split from its closest relatives over 20 million years ago, making it ecologically and biogeographically significant.
• [Issue] Bondo and Porja Adivasis, who have protested for two years, have applied for forest rights over the hill, which the government has refused to recognise.
• [Counterpoint] Sightings are few and the species' behaviour, habits and lifecycle remain unknown, so impact assessments rest on limited data.
• [Way forward] Recognise community forest rights before clearance, survey the gecko's habitat independently and treat the site as a no-go area.

CA Topic / Headline: Thailand deliberately floods riverside communities in Ayutthaya to spare Bangkok and industrial zones; a $780-million diversion canal for 1,200 cubic metres per second is due by 2030, while irrigation officials admit new embankments worsen downstream flooding.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):

CA Topic / Headline: Microsoft Quantum's Majorana 2 processor, announced June 2, replaces aluminium with lead and shows a topological gap rising from about 30 to 70 microelectron-volts; physicists, including Sergey Frolov, remain sceptical of whether the qubits are working topological qubits.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• Majorana 1, announced in February 2025, contained eight qubits built on a 'topoconductor' of indium-arsenide-aluminium; Microsoft said future chips would hold a million qubits.
• Majorana zero modes are emergent quasiparticles predicted by Sankar Das Sarma, Roman Lutchyn and Jay Sau in 2010 at ends of engineered superconducting wires.
• Majorana 2 uses lead instead of aluminium, a gallium-antimonide substrate and a redesigned stack; parity switching time rose from a few milliseconds to about 20 seconds.
• Microsoft says it will build a scalable quantum computer by 2029; Nature published a rebuttal by Henry Legg on June 24 alongside a response from Microsoft.
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Issue] Impostor states mimic Majorana zero modes, so inference from device properties must be airtight; the dispute is that Microsoft's inference is not.
• [Counterpoint] A 2018 TU Delft Nature paper claiming Majorana zero modes was retracted three years later, showing the field's record of premature claims.
• [Counterpoint] Many physicists commend Microsoft's transparency with data and find its attempts promising, though many remain unconvinced that the qubits are working topological qubits.
• [Way forward] Independent replication, open data and agreed benchmarks should precede commercial claims about quantum hardware.
